questions.topic: Work and Kinetic Energy - Earth's Orbital Kinetic Energy
questions.q: Determine the kinetic energy associated with the revolution of the Earth around the Sun, given that the mass of the Earth is $m_E = 5.98 \cdot 10^{24}\text{ kg}$, the mean orbital radius of Earth's orbit is $R = 1.50 \cdot 10^{11}\text{ m}$, and the period of revolution is $T = 3.16 \cdot 10^7\text{ s}$.
questions.hint: First calculate the tangential orbital velocity $v = \frac{2\pi R}{T}$. Then apply the kinetic energy formula $K = \frac{1}{2} m_E v^2$.
explanations: Correct! The orbital velocity is $v = \frac{2\pi (1.50 \cdot 10^{11})}{3.16 \cdot 10^7} \approx 29825\text{ m/s}$. The kinetic energy is $K = \frac{1}{2} (5.98 \cdot 10^{24}) \cdot (29825)^2 \approx 2.66 \cdot 10^{33}\text{ J} \approx 2.7 \cdot 10^{33}\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. Result doubled due to forgetting to divide by $2$ in the formula for $K$.
Incorrect. Error in conversion or in squaring the velocity.
Incorrect. Value obtained by squaring the Earth's mass instead of the velocity.

questions.topic: Mechanical Work - Force Incline on a Horizontal Plane
questions.q: To push a $50\text{ kg}$ crate across a frictionless horizontal floor, a porter applies a force of $210\text{ N}$ directed $20^\circ$ above the horizontal. During a displacement of $3.0\text{ m}$, determine the total work done on the crate.
questions.hint: The work done by the applied force is $W = F \cdot d \cdot \cos\theta$. Weight and normal force are perpendicular to displacement, so they do zero work. Total work equals work done by applied force.
explanations: Correct! Work done by porter's force is $W = 210 \cdot 3.0 \cdot \cos(20^\circ) = 630 \cdot 0.9397 \approx 592\text{ J}$. Since weight and normal reaction force form a $90^\circ$ angle with horizontal displacement, their work is $0\text{ J}$. Thus total work is $592\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $630\text{ J}$ is obtained by ignoring the force inclination angle (assuming $\cos 0^\circ = 1$).
Incorrect. $215\text{ J}$ is obtained by incorrectly multiplying by $\sin 20^\circ$.
Incorrect. Total work is not zero because a horizontal force component parallel to displacement exists.

questions.topic: Inclined Plane Dynamics - Force at Constant Velocity
questions.q: A $45\text{ kg}$ block of ice slides down an inclined plane that is $1.5\text{ m}$ long and $0.91\text{ m}$ high. A handler pushes up from below against the block with a force parallel to the incline so that it moves down at constant velocity. What is the magnitude of the force exerted by the handler?
questions.hint: Since velocity is constant, acceleration is zero and net force parallel to incline is zero. The handler's force balances the component of weight parallel to incline $F_{||} = m g \sin\theta = m g \frac{h}{L}$.
explanations: Correct! Parallel component of weight is $F_{||} = m g \frac{h}{L} = 45 \cdot 9.81 \cdot \frac{0.91}{1.5} \approx 267.8\text{ N} \approx 268\text{ N}$. To maintain constant velocity, upward parallel force by handler must be $268\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. $441\text{ N}$ is total weight of block ($m g$).
Incorrect. $402$ is work done in Joules, not force magnitude in Newtons.
Incorrect. Error in incline trigonometric ratio calculation.

questions.topic: Mechanical Work - Work Done by Gravity on Inclined Plane
questions.q: For the same $45\text{ kg}$ ice block sliding down the $0.91\text{ m}$ high inclined plane, what is the work done by gravity during the entire descent?
questions.hint: Work done by gravity depends solely on vertical height difference $h$: $W_{gravity} = m g h$.
explanations: Correct! Since block moves down vertically by $h = 0.91\text{ m}$, gravity work is positive: $W_{gravity} = m g h = 45 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 0.91 \approx 401.7\text{ J} \approx 402\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $-402\text{ J}$ is resistive work done by handler pushing opposite to motion.
Incorrect. $268\text{ J}$ is magnitude of handler force in Newtons.
Incorrect. Work done by gravity is non-zero because vertical displacement occurred.

questions.topic: Work and Conservative Forces - Cable Hoist
questions.q: A helicopter rescues a $72\text{ kg}$ astronaut from the ocean, lifting them by $15\text{ m}$ with upward acceleration $a = g/10$. Determine work $W_{helicopter}$ done by cable and work $W_{gravity}$ done by weight of astronaut.
questions.hint: Cable tension is $T = m(g + a) = m(1.1 g)$. Cable work is $W_{helicopter} = T \cdot h$. Gravity work is resistive: $W_{gravity} = -m g h$.
explanations: Correct! Using $g = 9.81\text{ m/s}^2$: weight force is $F_p = 72 \cdot 9.81 = 706.32\text{ N}$, yielding $W_{gravity} = -706.32 \cdot 15 = -10594.8\text{ J} \approx -10590\text{ J}$. Cable tension is $T = 72 \cdot (1.1 \cdot 9.81) = 776.95\text{ N}$, yielding $W_{helicopter} = 776.95 \cdot 15 \approx 11655\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $10590\text{ J}$ for helicopter corresponds to constant speed lift ($a=0$).
Incorrect. $1065\text{ J}$ is net work or kinetic energy change of astronaut.
Incorrect. Gravity work is non-zero during vertical displacement.

questions.topic: Work-Energy Theorem - Final Hoist Velocity
questions.q: Using data from previous problem ($m = 72\text{ kg}$, $h = 15\text{ m}$, $a = g/10$), determine kinetic energy $K$ and speed $v$ of astronaut just before reaching helicopter.
questions.hint: Final kinetic energy equals total net work $K = W_{tot} = W_{helicopter} + W_{gravity} = m a h$. Speed derived from $v = \sqrt{2 a h}$.
explanations: Correct! Net work is $W_{tot} = 11655\text{ J} - 10590\text{ J} = 1065\text{ J}$, corresponding to final kinetic energy $K$. Final velocity is $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 K}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot 1065}{72}} = \sqrt{29.58} \approx 5.44\text{ m/s} \approx 5.4\text{ m/s}$. Alternatively via kinematics $v = \sqrt{2 a h} = \sqrt{2 \cdot 0.981 \cdot 15} \approx 5.4\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $11655\text{ J}$ is work done by cable alone, not net kinetic energy.
Incorrect. $10590\text{ J}$ is absolute magnitude of gravity work.
Incorrect. Halving error in calculation of kinetic energy.

questions.topic: Mechanical Power - Fully Loaded Elevator
questions.q: An elevator cab has a mass of $4500\text{ kg}$ and maximum payload of $1800\text{ kg}$. Elevator rises fully loaded at constant speed $3.8\text{ m/s}$. What power must be delivered to maintain this speed?
questions.hint: First calculate total mass $M = m_{cab} + m_{payload}$. Force needed to ascend at constant velocity equals total weight $F = M \cdot g$. Required power $P = F \cdot v$.
explanations: Correct! Total mass is $M = 4500 + 1800 = 6300\text{ kg}$. Tension force needed to balance weight at constant speed is $F = 6300 \cdot 9.81 = 61803\text{ N}$. Power is $P = 61803 \cdot 3.8 = 234851\text{ W} \approx 235\text{ kW}$.
Incorrect. $168\text{ kW}$ calculated using cab mass only without payload.
Incorrect. $67\text{ kW}$ considers payload only excluding cab mass.
Incorrect. $61.8\text{ kW}$ corresponds to weight force magnitude in kN without multiplying by velocity $v$.

questions.topic: Mechanical Power - Drag Proportional to Velocity
questions.q: The force required to tow a boat at constant speed is directly proportional to speed ($F \propto v$). If $10\text{ kW}$ of power is needed for $4\text{ km/h}$, find power needed for $12\text{ km/h}$.
questions.hint: Since $F = b \cdot v$, power is $P = F \cdot v = b \cdot v^2$. Power is proportional to square of velocity ($P \propto v^2$).
explanations: Correct! Tripling velocity from $4\text{ km/h}$ to $12\text{ km/h}$ ($k = 3$), since power scales with square of speed ($P \propto v^2$), power increases by factor of $3^2 = 9$. Thus $P_2 = 9 \cdot 10\text{ kW} = 90\text{ kW}$.
Incorrect. $30\text{ kW}$ assumes linear dependency on velocity rather than quadratic.
Incorrect. $270\text{ kW}$ occurs if force scales quadratically ($F \propto v^2 \implies P \propto v^3$).
Incorrect. Calculation error in proportion.

questions.topic: Power Theory - Fluid Drag Dependence on Velocity
questions.q: If fluid resistance on a moving body is proportional to velocity ($F = b \cdot v$), how does engine power delivered to maintain uniform linear motion vary with speed $v$?
questions.hint: Recall instantaneous power definition $P = F \cdot v$. Substitute force expression into power equation.
options: Increases with the square of velocity ($P \propto v^2$)
Increases directly proportional to velocity ($P \propto v$)
Increases with the cube of velocity ($P \propto v^3$)
explanations: Correct! Power is defined as $P = F \cdot v$. Substituting $F = b \cdot v$ gives $P = b \cdot v^2$. Thus power spent increases quadratically with velocity.
Incorrect. Power depends linearly on speed only if drag force is constant.
Incorrect. Power varies with cube of velocity ($P \propto v^3$) when force varies quadratically ($F \propto v^2$), typical of high-speed aerodynamic drag.
Incorrect. Overcoming an increasing resistive force requires higher power delivery.

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy - Equilibrium of Suspended Mass
questions.q: A spring with constant $k = 2300\text{ N/m}$ hangs vertically from a ceiling at rest. A mass $m$ attached to it stretches it to equilibrium position, imparting elastic potential energy $U_e = 14\text{ J}$. What is mass $m$?
questions.hint: At equilibrium spring force balances weight: $k x = m g \implies x = \frac{m g}{k}$. Elastic potential energy is $U_e = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{m^2 g^2}{2 k}$. Isolate $m$.
explanations: Correct! From equilibrium energy formula $U_e = \frac{m^2 g^2}{2 k}$, $m^2 = \frac{2 k U_e}{g^2} = \frac{2 \cdot 2300 \cdot 14}{(9.81)^2} \approx \frac{64400}{96.236} \approx 669.2$. Taking square root: $m = \sqrt{669.2} \approx 25.87\text{ kg} \approx 26\text{ kg}$.
Incorrect. $13\text{ kg}$ obtained by omitting factor of $2$ in elastic energy formula.
Incorrect. $670\text{ kg}$ corresponds to $m^2$ prior to square root.
Incorrect. Error in setting up weight equilibrium condition.

questions.topic: Work of Elastic Force - Stretching a Spring
questions.q: A spring with constant $k = 7.7\text{ N/m}$ rests at origin of horizontal axis. Calculate work required to stretch spring from position $x_1 = +5\text{ cm}$ to $x_2 = +9\text{ cm}$.
questions.hint: Convert positions to meters ($x_1 = 0.05\text{ m}$, $x_2 = 0.09\text{ m}$). External work required equals elastic potential energy change $\Delta U_e = \frac{1}{2} k x_2^2 - \frac{1}{2} k x_1^2$.
explanations: Correct! Expressing in meters: $x_1 = 0.05\text{ m}$ and $x_2 = 0.09\text{ m}$. Work is $\Delta U_e = \frac{1}{2} k (x_2^2 - x_1^2) = \frac{1}{2} (7.7) (0.09^2 - 0.05^2) = 3.85 \cdot (0.0081 - 0.0025) = 3.85 \cdot 0.0056 = 0.02156\text{ J} \approx 0.022\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $0.015\text{ J}$ calculated incorrectly using $\frac{1}{2} k (x_2 - x_1)^2 = \frac{1}{2} (7.7) (0.04)^2$.
Incorrect. Error in omitting position squaring.
Incorrect. $0.22\text{ J}$ stems from failing to convert centimeters to meters.

questions.topic: Conservative Forces Theory - Work of Elastic Force
questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding work done by elastic force $F_e = -k x$ is CORRECT?
questions.hint: Reflect on conservative nature of spring force and potential energy definition.
options: Elastic force is conservative, so its work depends only on initial and final positions of spring
Elastic force is non-conservative, so its work depends on path taken to deform it
Work done by elastic force is always positive, regardless of displacement direction
Work done by elastic force along closed path is always non-zero
explanations: Correct! Elastic force is conservative; work done by it equals negative change in potential energy $W_{el} = -\Delta U_e = \frac{1}{2}k x_i^2 - \frac{1}{2}k x_f^2$, depending solely on initial and final points.
Incorrect. Elastic force is conservative, not dissipative.
Incorrect. Elastic force work is negative when spring is stretched away from equilibrium position (force and displacement opposite).
Incorrect. For any conservative force, work done over closed path is exactly zero.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - Trampoline Spring Constant
questions.q: At a playground, a man of mass $m = 80\text{ kg}$ leaps onto a trampoline from height $h = 10\text{ m}$ above rest level. Upon landing, trampoline deforms downward by $y = 1.75\text{ m}$. Neglecting dissipative forces, determine trampoline spring constant $k$.
questions.hint: Apply mechanical energy conservation between start point and maximum compression point. Total height drop is $H = h + y = 11.75\text{ m}$, so $m g (h + y) = \frac{1}{2} k y^2$.
explanations: Correct! Total vertical distance is $H = 10 + 1.75 = 11.75\text{ m}$. All gravitational potential energy converts to elastic potential energy: $m g H = \frac{1}{2} k y^2 \implies 80 \cdot 9.81 \cdot 11.75 = \frac{1}{2} k (1.75)^2 \implies 9221.4 = 1.53125 k \implies k \approx 6022\text{ N/m} \approx 6 \cdot 10^3\text{ N/m}$.
Incorrect. $5 \cdot 10^3\text{ N/m}$ considers height $h = 10\text{ m}$ only, ignoring extra displacement $y = 1.75\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. Calculation error in squaring deformation $y$.
Incorrect. Obtained by mistakenly doubling spring constant value.

questions.topic: Work of Non-Conservative Forces - Inelastic Rebound
questions.q: Using data from previous problem ($m = 80\text{ kg}$, initial height $h = 10\text{ m}$), knowing man rebounds up to final height $h_f = 3\text{ m}$ above trampoline rest level, determine work $W_{nc}$ done by non-conservative forces.
questions.hint: Work by non-conservative forces equals total mechanical energy change: $W_{nc} = \Delta E_{mech} = E_{final} - E_{initial} = m g h_f - m g h_i$.
explanations: Correct! Potential (mechanical) energy change is $W_{nc} = m g (h_f - h_i) = 80 \cdot 9.81 \cdot (3 - 10) = 784.8 \cdot (-7) = -5493.6\text{ J} \approx -5.5 \cdot 10^3\text{ J}$. Negative sign indicates mechanical energy dissipation.
Incorrect. Work done by dissipative forces here must be negative due to energy loss.
Incorrect. $2.4 \cdot 10^3\text{ J}$ calculated considering final energy at $3\text{ m}$ height only.
Incorrect. $7.8 \cdot 10^3\text{ J}$ corresponds to initial energy at $10\text{ m}$ height.

questions.topic: Inclined Plane, Friction and Spring - Minimum Drop Height
questions.q: A point mass $m = 20\text{ g}$ sits at height $h$ above a smooth incline. Released from rest, it slides down incline and continues onto rough horizontal track of length $d = 40\text{ cm}$ with friction coefficient $\mu = 0.1$, reaching spring with constant $k = 2\text{ N/m}$ and relaxed length $10\text{ cm}$. Determine initial height $h$ so mass fully compresses spring to wall.
questions.hint: Initial potential energy $m g h$ must equal friction work over $40\text{ cm}$ ($W_{fric} = \mu m g d$) plus elastic potential energy of fully compressed spring over $x = 10\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ m}$ ($U_e = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$).
explanations: Correct! Converting to SI ($m = 0.02\text{ kg}$, $d = 0.40\text{ m}$, $x = 0.10\text{ m}$): $m g h = \mu m g d + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 \implies h = \mu d + \frac{k x^2}{2 m g} = 0.1 \cdot 0.40 + \frac{2 \cdot (0.10)^2}{2 \cdot 0.02 \cdot 9.81} = 0.04\text{ m} + \frac{0.02}{0.3924}\text{ m} \approx 0.04 + 0.051 = 0.091\text{ m} = 9.1\text{ cm}$.
Incorrect. $5.1\text{ cm}$ considers height needed to compress spring only, ignoring horizontal friction losses.
Incorrect. $10.1\text{ cm}$ calculates friction over full $50\text{ cm}$ length ($40\text{ cm} + 10\text{ cm}$).
Incorrect. Error in converting mass from grams to kilograms.

questions.topic: Mechanical Energy Conservation - Energy Balance with Friction
questions.q: In a mechanical system with conservative forces (gravity, spring) and dissipative forces (kinetic friction), which equation correctly expresses energy balance between initial state (rest at height $h$) and final state (rest after rough distance $d$ and compressing spring distance $x$)?
questions.hint: Initial mechanical energy $E_i$ partially converts to final energy $E_f$ and partially dissipates as negative work of friction $|W_{fric}|$.
options: $m g h = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 + \mu m g d$
$m g h + \frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \mu m g d$
$m g h = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 - \mu m g d$
$m g h = k x + \mu m g$
explanations: Correct! By mechanical energy theorem, $E_i + W_{nc} = E_f \implies m g h - \mu m g d = \frac{1}{2} k x^2$, which rearranges to $m g h = \frac{1}{2} k x^2 + \mu m g d$.
Incorrect. Spring potential energy belongs on final state side.
Incorrect. Work against friction is positive term added to final required energy to balance initial energy.
Incorrect. Elastic energy depends on squared compression $\frac{1}{2} k x^2$ and friction work on distance $d$.

questions.topic: Potential Energy and Work - Relation for Conservative Forces
questions.q: A single conservative force $F$ acts on a particle. At point $A$, potential energy is $U_A = 40\text{ J}$. Moving particle from $A$ to $B$, force $F$ does work $W_{A \to B} = +25\text{ J}$. What is potential energy $U_B$ at point $B$?
questions.hint: For conservative forces, work relates to potential energy change via $W_{A \to B} = -\Delta U = U_A - U_B$.
explanations: Correct! Since $W_{A \to B} = U_A - U_B$, substituting values gives $25 = 40 - U_B \implies U_B = 40 - 25 = 15\text{ J}$. Positive work by conservative force lowers potential energy.
Incorrect. $65\text{ J}$ obtained by adding work to initial potential energy ($U_B = U_A + W$).
Incorrect. $-15\text{ J}$ comes from sign error in potential energy change formula.
Incorrect. $25\text{ J}$ is work done by force, not final potential energy.

questions.topic: Theory - Work Properties of Conservative Force
questions.q: If conservative force does positive work ($W_{A \to B} > 0$) moving particle from point $A$ to $B$, what holds true regarding potential energy $U$?
questions.hint: Recall work of conservative force measures potential energy decrease: $W_{A \to B} = -\Delta U$.
options: Potential energy of system decreases ($U_B < U_A$)
Potential energy of system increases ($U_B > U_A$)
Potential energy of system remains unchanged ($U_B = U_A$)
explanations: Correct! By conservative force definition $W = -\Delta U = U_A - U_B$. If $W > 0$, then $U_A - U_B > 0 \implies U_B < U_A$, meaning potential energy decreases.
Incorrect. Potential energy increases only if work done is negative ($W < 0$).
Incorrect. Potential energy unchanged only if work is zero ($W = 0$).
Incorrect. Work determines potential energy change, not its absolute value.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - Initial Potential Energy
questions.q: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ book is dropped toward arms of person $10\text{ m}$ below starting point (height $h_1 = 10\text{ m}$ above ground). Setting zero potential energy at ground, what is initial potential energy $U_1$ of book when fall starts?
questions.hint: Apply gravitational potential energy definition $U = m \cdot g \cdot h$ considering height relative to ground.
explanations: Correct! Gravitational potential energy relative to ground: $U_1 = m \cdot g \cdot h_1 = 2.0 \cdot 9.8 \cdot 10 = 196\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $29.4\text{ J}$ corresponds to book potential energy at final hand height ($1.5\text{ m}$ from ground).
Incorrect. $166.6\text{ J}$ is kinetic energy gained during fall before impact.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - Kinetic Energy Before Impact
questions.q: For the $2.0\text{ kg}$ book dropped from height $10\text{ m}$, calculate its kinetic energy $K$ just before being caught by hands at height $h_2 = 1.5\text{ m}$ above ground.
questions.hint: Kinetic energy before impact equals potential energy drop: $K = U_1 - U_2 = m g (h_1 - h_2)$.
explanations: Correct! Book loses potential energy descending from $10\text{ m}$ to $1.5\text{ m}$ (drop $\Delta h = 8.5\text{ m}$). By energy conservation: $K = m \cdot g \cdot \Delta h = 2.0 \cdot 9.8 \cdot 8.5 = 166.6\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $29.4\text{ J}$ is remaining potential energy at height $1.5\text{ m}$, not accumulated kinetic energy.
Incorrect. $196\text{ J}$ is total initial potential energy.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - Falling Velocity
questions.q: Calculate speed $v$ of $2.0\text{ kg}$ book at impact with hands at $1.5\text{ m}$ above ground (knowing kinetic energy is $K = 166.6\text{ J}$).
questions.hint: Use kinetic energy formula $K = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$ and isolate speed $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 K}{m}}$.
explanations: Correct! Isolating speed: $v = \sqrt{\frac{2 K}{m}} = \sqrt{\frac{2 \cdot 166.6}{2.0}} = \sqrt{166.6} \approx 12.9\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Error caused by using gravitational acceleration $g$ instead of velocity formula.
Incorrect. Error in square root calculation or kinetic energy setup.

questions.topic: Mechanical Energy Conservation - Safety Net Stretch
questions.q: A $70.0\text{ kg}$ man jumps from window into firefighter net stretched $11.0\text{ m}$ below. Net sags $1.5\text{ m}$, bringing him to rest before bouncing upward. Calculate maximum net potential energy assuming mechanical energy conservation.
questions.hint: Total vertical drop is fall height plus net sagging: $H = h + \Delta x = 11.0 + 1.5 = 12.5\text{ m}$. All gravitational potential energy converts to net elastic energy.
explanations: Correct! Total drop distance is $H = 11.0 + 1.5 = 12.5\text{ m}$. Gravitational potential energy converted to net elasticity is $U = m \cdot g \cdot H = 70.0 \cdot 9.8 \cdot 12.5 = 8575\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $7546\text{ J}$ considers fall height $11.0\text{ m}$ only, ignoring $1.5\text{ m}$ net sagging.
Incorrect. $1029\text{ J}$ corresponds to potential energy associated with $1.5\text{ m}$ sagging only.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - Tanker Truck Emergency Ramp
questions.q: An runaway tanker truck moves at $130\text{ km/h}$ when entering emergency uphill ramp inclined at $15^\circ$. Find minimum ramp length $L$ for truck to stop momentarily (ignoring friction).
questions.hint: Convert speed to $\text{m/s}$ ($v = \frac{130}{3.6} \approx 36.11\text{ m/s}$). Equate kinetic energy to maximum height potential energy: $\frac{1}{2} m v^2 = m g h \implies h = \frac{v^2}{2g}$. Ramp length $L = \frac{h}{\sin 15^\circ}$.
explanations: Correct! Speed $v = 36.11\text{ m/s}$. Height to stop truck $h = \frac{v^2}{2g} \approx 66.5\text{ m}$. Distance along ramp incline $L = \frac{h}{\sin 15^\circ} \approx \frac{66.5}{0.2588} \approx 248\text{ m}$.
Incorrect. $130\text{ m}$ is speed value in $\text{km/h}$, not ramp length.
Incorrect. Error from omitting angle sine in ramp geometric component setup.

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy - Popgun at Equilibrium Position
questions.q: Spring force of popgun is $F = -10 \Delta x$ ($F$ in $\text{N}$, $\Delta x$ in $\text{m}$, so $k = 10\text{ N/m}$). Spring is compressed $x_1 = 5.5\text{ cm}$ to fire cork of mass $m = 3.8\text{ g}$. Find cork speed as spring passes equilibrium position ($x = 0$).
questions.hint: Convert $x_1 = 0.055\text{ m}$ and $m = 0.0038\text{ kg}$. All initial elastic potential energy converts to kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} k x_1^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$.
explanations: Correct! Equating elastic energy to kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} k x_1^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \implies v = x_1 \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = 0.055 \sqrt{\frac{10}{0.0038}} = 0.055 \cdot 51.3 \approx 2.82\text{ m/s} \approx 2.8\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $1.5\text{ m/s}$ obtained from mass conversion errors (grams to kilograms).
Incorrect. Error in calculating compression scale factor expressed in centimeters.

questions.topic: Elastic Potential Energy - Popgun Release upon Extension
questions.q: For same popgun ($k = 10\text{ N/m}$, initial compression $x_1 = 5.5\text{ cm}$, mass $m = 3.8\text{ g}$), assuming cork stays attached to spring and detaches after stretching it by $x_2 = 1.5\text{ cm}$, find cork speed at release.
questions.hint: Final state spring still retains elastic potential energy. Energy balance: $\frac{1}{2} k x_1^2 = \frac{1}{2} k x_2^2 + \frac{1}{2} m v_2^2 \implies v_2 = \sqrt{\frac{k(x_1^2 - x_2^2)}{m}}$.
explanations: Correct! Converting to meters: $x_1 = 0.055\text{ m}$ and $x_2 = 0.015\text{ m}$. Speed calculation: $v = \sqrt{\frac{10 \cdot (0.055^2 - 0.015^2)}{0.0038}} = \sqrt{\frac{10 \cdot (0.003025 - 0.000225)}{0.0038}} = \sqrt{\frac{0.028}{0.0038}} \approx 2.71\text{ m/s} \approx 2.7\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Error in subtracting deformation amplitudes $(x_1 - x_2)^2$ instead of their squares $(x_1^2 - x_2^2)$.
Incorrect. Obtained by adding energies instead of subtracting in energy balance.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - Spring Detachment Velocity
questions.q: A mass $m = 200\text{ g}$ is pushed left against spring of constant $k = 400\text{ N/m}$, compressing it by $x = 15\text{ cm}$ from equilibrium. Released, mass shoots right. Neglecting friction and spring mass, at what speed $v$ will mass move when detaching from spring?
questions.hint: Equate initial elastic potential energy $\frac{1}{2} k x^2$ to final kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2} m v^2$. Convert mass to $\text{kg}$ ($m = 0.2\text{ kg}$) and compression to meters ($x = 0.15\text{ m}$).
explanations: Correct! Converting to SI ($m = 0.2\text{ kg}$, $x = 0.15\text{ m}$), elastic energy converts to kinetic energy: $\frac{1}{2} k x^2 = \frac{1}{2} m v^2 \implies v = x \sqrt{\frac{k}{m}} = 0.15 \sqrt{\frac{400}{0.2}} = 0.15 \sqrt{2000} \approx 6.71\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. Obtained by forgetting to square stretch or velocity term.
Incorrect. Calculation error converting mass from grams to kilograms.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - New Maximum Compression
questions.q: Assuming instead mass $m = 200\text{ g}$ moves left at initial speed $v_0 = 8\text{ m/s}$ and sticks to spring upon impact, calculate new maximum compression $x_{\text{max}}$ of spring (oscillation amplitude).
questions.hint: Initial kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2$ converts fully to elastic potential energy $\frac{1}{2} k x_{\text{max}}^2$ at maximum compression.
explanations: Correct! By energy conservation: $\frac{1}{2} m v_0^2 = \frac{1}{2} k x_{\text{max}}^2 \implies x_{\text{max}} = v_0 \sqrt{\frac{m}{k}} = 8 \sqrt{\frac{0.2}{400}} = 8 \sqrt{0.0005} \approx 0.1789\text{ m} = 17.9\text{ cm}$.
Incorrect. Error using mass in grams instead of kilograms.
Incorrect. Obtained by forgetting to take square root of ratio $m/k$.

questions.topic: Inclined Plane and Static Friction - Equilibrium Condition
questions.q: A crate rests on a rough incline at angle $\theta = 30^\circ$ relative to horizontal. What is minimum static friction coefficient $\mu_s$ to prevent crate from sliding down?
questions.hint: For equilibrium, maximum static friction force must balance parallel weight component: $\mu_s m g \cos 30^\circ \ge m g \sin 30^\circ \implies \mu_s \ge \tan 30^\circ$.
explanations: Correct! Incline equilibrium occurs when friction force $F_s = \mu_s m g \cos 30^\circ$ equals parallel force component $F_p = m g \sin 30^\circ$. Dividing gives $\mu_s = \tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.577 \approx 0.58$.
Incorrect. $0.50$ equals $\sin 30^\circ$, not angle tangent.
Incorrect. $0.87$ equals $\cos 30^\circ$, miscalculating weight components ratio.

questions.topic: Statics and Static Friction - Friction Coefficient Calculation
questions.q: A force $F = 50\text{ N}$ inclined at $60^\circ$ above horizontal is applied to body of mass $m = 5\text{ kg}$ on rough horizontal plane. Given maximum static friction force is $F_s = 40\text{ N}$, calculate static friction coefficient $\mu_s$.
questions.hint: Static friction coefficient calculated considering maximum friction force relative to normal weight force: $\mu_s = \frac{F_s}{m g}$.
explanations: Correct! Static friction coefficient derived from $\mu_s = \frac{F_s}{m g} = \frac{40}{5 \cdot 9.8} = \frac{40}{49} \approx 0.816 \approx 0.82$.
Incorrect. $0.50$ is cosine component of applied force angle.
Incorrect. Error in dividing applied force by weight instead of using maximum friction force.

questions.topic: Statics and Static Friction - Verification of Motion
questions.q: A body of mass $m = 5\text{ kg}$ on a horizontal plane is acted upon by a force $F = 50\text{ N}$ applied at an angle of $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. If the maximum static friction force is $F_s = 40\text{ N}$, will the body start moving?
questions.hint: Compare horizontal component of applied force $F_x = F \cos 60^\circ$ with maximum static friction force $F_s = 40\text{ N}$.
options: No, body remains at rest because horizontal component $F_x = 25\text{ N}$ is less than maximum static friction $F_s = 40\text{ N}$.
Yes, body moves because total applied force magnitude $F = 50\text{ N}$ is greater than $F_s = 40\text{ N}$.
Yes, body moves because vertical component completely cancels body weight.
explanations: Correct! Horizontal component responsible for sliding is $F_x = F \cos 60^\circ = 50 \cdot 0.5 = 25\text{ N}$. Since $F_x = 25\text{ N} < 40\text{ N}$, applied force fails to overcome static friction and body remains motionless.
Incorrect. Do not compare total force magnitude $F$, but only horizontal component in direction of motion.
Incorrect. Vertical component $F_y = 50 \sin 60^\circ \approx 43.3\text{ N}$ is less than weight $P = 49\text{ N}$, so body maintains contact with plane.

questions.topic: Dynamics and Friction - Deceleration due to Sliding Friction
questions.q: A car moves at constant speed when put into neutral (engine disengaged). Friction coefficient between tires and asphalt is $\mu = 0.5$. If no other force acts, what acceleration $a$ will car experience?
questions.hint: Only acting horizontal force is kinetic friction $F_a = -\mu m g$. Applying Newton's second law ($F = m a$), mass cancels out leaving $a = -\mu g$.
explanations: Correct! Only friction force acts on car $F_a = -\mu m g$. By Newton's second law: $m a = -\mu m g \implies a = -\mu g = -0.5 \cdot 9.8\text{ m/s}^2 = -4.9\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. $-0.5\text{ m/s}^2$ corresponds only to dimensionless friction coefficient $\mu$, without multiplication by gravity acceleration $g$.
Incorrect. $-9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ is gravitational acceleration $g$, obtained only with friction coefficient $\mu = 1$.

questions.topic: Inclined Plane with Friction - Stopping Distance
questions.q: A body of mass $m = 1\text{ kg}$ is launched upward along a rough incline with friction coefficient $\mu = 0.2$. Initial velocity is $v_0 = 3\text{ m/s}$ and incline angle is $\theta = 30^\circ$ relative to horizontal. Determine distance $d$ traveled along incline before stopping.
questions.hint: Deceleration during ascent is $a = g (\sin 30^\circ + \mu \cos 30^\circ)$. Then use kinematic formula $v_0^2 = 2 a d$.
explanations: Correct! Total deceleration along incline is $a = g(\sin 30^\circ + \mu \cos 30^\circ) = 9.8 \cdot (0.5 + 0.2 \cdot 0.866) \approx 6.60\text{ m/s}^2$. Stopping distance $d = \frac{v_0^2}{2a} = \frac{3^2}{2 \cdot 6.60} \approx 0.682\text{ m} \approx 68\text{ cm}$.
Incorrect. $92\text{ cm}$ assumes perfectly smooth incline (no friction), considering gravity component $g \sin 30^\circ$ only.
Incorrect. Error in combining signs or calculating normal weight component.

questions.topic: Conservation of Momentum - Release of Spring Between Two Masses
questions.q: Two blocks of mass $M$ and $3M$ rest on a frictionless horizontal plane with a compressed spring between them, held by cord. When cord is cut, block of mass $3M$ moves right at velocity $v_{3M} = 2\text{ m/s}$. What is velocity $v_M$ of block of mass $M$?
questions.hint: Apply total momentum conservation law (initially zero): $p_i = 0 \implies p_f = M v_M + 3M v_{3M} = 0$.
explanations: Correct! From momentum conservation: $0 = M v_M + 3M v_{3M} \implies v_M = -3 v_{3M} = -3 \cdot 2 = -6\text{ m/s}$. Negative sign indicates velocity directed left.
Incorrect. Since masses differ ($M$ and $3M$), they cannot move at same speed while conserving momentum.
Incorrect. Result obtained by mistakenly multiplying by squared mass ratio.

questions.topic: Energy Conservation - Elastic Potential Energy
questions.q: Using data from previous problem ($M = 0.35\text{ kg}$, $v_{3M} = 2\text{ m/s}$, $v_M = 6\text{ m/s}$), find elastic potential energy $U_e$ initially stored in compressed spring.
questions.hint: Initial spring elastic potential energy converts entirely to total kinetic energy of two-block system: $U_e = \frac{1}{2} M v_M^2 + \frac{1}{2} (3M) v_{3M}^2$.
explanations: Correct! Calculating kinetic energy of both blocks: $U_e = \frac{1}{2} M v_M^2 + \frac{1}{2} (3M) v_{3M}^2 = \frac{1}{2} (0.35) (6^2) + \frac{1}{2} (3 \cdot 0.35) (2^2) = 6.30 + 2.10 = 8.40\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $6.30\text{ J}$ is kinetic energy acquired by block of mass $M$ only.
Incorrect. $2.10\text{ J}$ represents kinetic energy acquired by block of mass $3M$ only.

questions.topic: Successive Elastic Collisions - Final Velocity of First Sphere
questions.q: Three spheres are arranged in a straight line. Two right spheres (masses $m = 2\text{ g}$ and $M = 3\text{ g}$) are initially stationary, while first left sphere (mass $m = 2\text{ g}$) approaches at velocity $v = 5\text{ m/s}$. Assuming all collisions are perfectly elastic, calculate final velocity $v_{1f}$ of first left sphere (mass $m$).
questions.hint: Analyze collision sequence: first sphere $m$ transfers velocity to second $m$; second $m$ collides with $M$ and rebounds left at $-1\text{ m/s}$; finally second sphere hits stationary first sphere again.
explanations: Correct! In first collision between equal masses $m$, first sphere stops and transfers $5\text{ m/s}$ to second. Second sphere hits $M = 3\text{ g}$ and rebounds back with $v'_2 = \frac{m-M}{m+M} v = \frac{2-3}{2+3}(5) = -1\text{ m/s}$. Moving back, second sphere hits stationary first sphere ($m$), transferring $-1\text{ m/s}$ velocity.
Incorrect. $0\text{ m/s}$ would be first sphere velocity immediately after first collision, but it experiences second collision rebound from second sphere.
Incorrect. Result derived from improper treatment of sequential elastic collision stages.

questions.topic: Successive Elastic Collisions - Final Velocity of Second Sphere
questions.q: Using data from three-sphere problem ($m = 2\text{ g}$, $m = 2\text{ g}$, $M = 3\text{ g}$), calculate final velocity $v_{2f}$ of middle second sphere (mass $m = 2\text{ g}$) after all collisions complete.
questions.hint: After second sphere rebounds from $M$ leftward at $-1\text{ m/s}$, it hits stationary first sphere $m$. Equal masses exchange velocities.
explanations: Correct! After rebounding off $M$ at $-1\text{ m/s}$, second sphere hits stationary first sphere ($m$). In elastic collision between identical masses, second sphere transfers all momentum to first and comes to rest ($v_{2f} = 0\text{ m/s}$).
Incorrect. $-1\text{ m/s}$ is intermediate velocity of second sphere right after collision with $M$, prior to hitting first sphere again.
Incorrect. $4\text{ m/s}$ is final velocity of third sphere of mass $M$.

questions.topic: Successive Elastic Collisions - Final Velocity of Third Sphere
questions.q: Using data from three-sphere problem ($m = 2\text{ g}$, $m = 2\text{ g}$, $M = 3\text{ g}$), calculate final velocity $v_{3f}$ of third right sphere (mass $M = 3\text{ g}$).
questions.hint: Third sphere undergoes 1D elastic collision from incoming second sphere at $v = 5\text{ m/s}$. Use stationary target formula: $v_{3f} = \frac{2m}{m+M} v$.
explanations: Correct! In collision between second sphere ($m = 2\text{ g}$) with velocity $5\text{ m/s}$ and stationary third sphere ($M = 3\text{ g}$), transmitted velocity is $v_{3f} = \frac{2m}{m+M} v = \frac{2 \cdot 2}{2+3} \cdot 5 = \frac{4}{5} \cdot 5 = 4\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $2\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained if third sphere mass were twice mass $m$.
Incorrect. $5\text{ m/s}$ is initial velocity of first sphere, but heavier mass $M$ receives lower velocity.

questions.topic: Conservation of Momentum and Kinetic Energy - Rear-End Collision
questions.q: Two cars of mass $m_1 = 3000\text{ kg}$ and $m_2 = 1400\text{ kg}$ collide in rear-end crash. First car moves at $v_{1i} = 44\text{ m/s}$ and hits second moving at $v_{2i} = 25\text{ m/s}$. If immediately after impact first car travels at $v_{1f} = 37\text{ m/s}$, what is kinetic energy $E_{k2}$ of second car?
questions.hint: First determine final velocity $v_{2f}$ via momentum conservation: $m_1 v_{1i} + m_2 v_{2i} = m_1 v_{1f} + m_2 v_{2f}$. Then calculate $E_{k2} = \frac{1}{2} m_2 v_{2f}^2$.
explanations: Correct! From momentum conservation: $3000(44) + 1400(25) = 3000(37) + 1400 v_{2f} \implies 167000 = 111000 + 1400 v_{2f} \implies v_{2f} = 40\text{ m/s}$. Kinetic energy is $E_{k2} = \frac{1}{2} \cdot 1400 \cdot (40)^2 = 1120000\text{ J} = 1.12 \cdot 10^6\text{ J} \approx 1.1 \cdot 10^6\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $4.37 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$ represents initial kinetic energy of second car before collision.
Incorrect. Error in omitting factor $\frac{1}{2}$ in kinetic energy formula.

questions.topic: Inelastic Collision - Final Velocity of Railroad Cars
questions.q: A railroad car of mass $m_1 = 8000\text{ kg}$ moving at velocity $20\text{ m/s}$ hits a second identical stationary car ($m_2 = 8000\text{ kg}$). After collision, cars couple together. Determine velocity $v_f$ of system immediately after collision.
questions.hint: Being completely inelastic collision, apply momentum conservation: $m_1 v_1 = (m_1 + m_2) v_f$.
explanations: Correct! Applying momentum conservation: $m_1 v_1 = (m_1 + m_2) v_f \implies v_f = \frac{m_1 v_1}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{8000 \cdot 20}{16000} = 10\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $20\text{ m/s}$ is velocity of first car before collision; after impact mass doubles so velocity halves.
Incorrect. Error in dividing initial velocity by four instead of two.

questions.topic: Inelastic Collision - Kinetic Energy Loss
questions.q: Referring to collision between two identical railroad cars ($m_1 = m_2 = 8000\text{ kg}$, $v_1 = 20\text{ m/s}$, $v_f = 10\text{ m/s}$), determine kinetic energy change (loss) $\Delta K$ following collision.
questions.hint: Calculate difference between final kinetic energy $K_f = \frac{1}{2} (m_1+m_2) v_f^2$ and initial $K_i = \frac{1}{2} m_1 v_1^2$.
explanations: Correct! Initial energy: $K_i = \frac{1}{2} (8000) (20)^2 = 1.6 \cdot 10^6\text{ J}$. Final energy: $K_f = \frac{1}{2} (16000) (10)^2 = 8 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$. Loss is $\Delta K = K_f - K_i = 8 \cdot 10^5 - 1.6 \cdot 10^6 = -8 \cdot 10^5\text{ J}$.
Incorrect. $-1.6 \cdot 10^6\text{ J}$ equals total initial system kinetic energy.
Incorrect. Error in calculating squared final or initial velocity.

questions.topic: Inelastic Collision and Work - Resistive Force of Ground
questions.q: A body of mass $m_1 = 4.0\text{ kg}$ falls from rest height $h = 1.0\text{ m}$ onto body of mass $m_2 = 2.0\text{ kg}$. Bodies stick together and penetrate ground beneath to depth $d = 2.0\text{ cm}$. Determine average force $F$ ground exerts on mass system to stop it.
questions.hint: Calculate velocity of $m_1$ before impact ($v_1 = \sqrt{2gh}$), then common velocity right after impact ($v_f = \frac{m_1 v_1}{m_1+m_2}$). Equate system kinetic energy to work done by ground force ($F \cdot d = K_f$).
explanations: Correct! Before impact: $v_1 = \sqrt{2 \cdot 9.8 \cdot 1} \approx 4.43\text{ m/s}$. After inelastic collision: $v_f = \frac{4}{6} v_1 \approx 2.95\text{ m/s}$. System kinetic energy $K_f = \frac{1}{2} (6.0) (2.95)^2 \approx 26.13\text{ J}$. Ground stopping force $F = \frac{K_f}{d} = \frac{26.13}{0.02} \approx 1306\text{ N} \approx 1.3 \cdot 10^3\text{ N}$.
Incorrect. Obtained by mistakenly doubling remaining post-collision kinetic energy.
Incorrect. Obtained by ignoring inelastic collision nature and considering unreduced original fall energy.

questions.topic: Inelastic Collision - Kinetic Energy Loss Percentage
questions.q: In problem of $4.0\text{ kg}$ body falling onto $2.0\text{ kg}$ body and sticking together, what percentage of kinetic energy is lost in inelastic collision relative to pre-impact energy?
questions.hint: Compare kinetic energy right after impact $K_f$ with pre-impact $K_i$: conserved fraction is $\frac{K_f}{K_i} = \frac{m_1}{m_1+m_2}$.
explanations: Correct! Conserved kinetic energy fraction post-collision is $\frac{K_f}{K_i} = \frac{m_1}{m_1 + m_2} = \frac{4}{6} = 66.7\%$. Consequently lost energy percentage during collision is $100\% - 66.7\% = 33.3\% \approx 33\%$.
Incorrect. $50\%$ would occur only if both masses were equal ($m_1 = m_2$).
Incorrect. $67\%$ represents conserved energy percentage, not lost percentage.

questions.topic: Conservation of Momentum - Initial Train Speed
questions.q: Four railroad cars, each of mass $m = 2.50 \cdot 10^4\text{ kg}$, are linked and move with engine off at velocity $v_i$ southward. A person uncouples first car and pushes it, raising its velocity to $4\text{ m/s}$ southward, while other three cars continue at $2\text{ m/s}$ southward. Determine initial velocity $v_i$ of four cars.
questions.hint: Apply momentum conservation law: $4m v_i = m v_1 + 3m v_{234}$.
explanations: Correct! From momentum conservation: $4m v_i = m(4) + 3m(2) \implies 4 v_i = 4 + 6 = 10 \implies v_i = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $3.0\text{ m/s}$ is simple arithmetic mean of final velocities ($4$ and $2$), without accounting for weighted mass of 3 remaining joined cars.
Incorrect. Calculation error in summing final momentum contributions.

questions.topic: Work-Energy Theorem - Work Done by Push
questions.q: Using data from previous problem ($m = 2.50 \cdot 10^4\text{ kg}$ per car, $v_i = 2.5\text{ m/s}$, $v_1 = 4\text{ m/s}$, $v_{234} = 2\text{ m/s}$), determine work $W$ done by person to separate and push cars.
questions.hint: Work done by person equals total system kinetic energy change: $W = K_f - K_i$.
explanations: Incorrect. Obtained by mistakenly doubling work needed to alter kinetic energy.
Incorrect. Error in subtracting partial kinetic energy terms.

questions.topic: Conservation of Momentum in 2D - Boiler Explosion
questions.q: A boiler resting on horizontal floor explodes into three pieces. Two pieces of equal mass $m$ fly off at same speed $v = 9\text{ m/s}$ in mutually perpendicular directions. Given third piece has three times mass of others ($M = 3m$), determine speed magnitude $v_3$ of third piece right after explosion.
questions.hint: Initial total momentum is zero. Momentum magnitude of first two orthogonal pieces is $\sqrt{(m v)^2 + (m v)^2} = m v \sqrt{2}$. Equate to momentum magnitude of third piece $3m v_3$.
explanations: Correct! Conserving momentum on two orthogonal axes: $3m v_3 = \sqrt{(m v)^2 + (m v)^2} = m v \sqrt{2} \implies v_3 = \frac{v \sqrt{2}}{3} = \frac{9 \sqrt{2}}{3} = 3 \sqrt{2} \approx 4.24\text{ m/s} \approx 4.2\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $6.0\text{ m/s}$ would be obtained by dividing arithmetic velocity sum ($18$) by three.
Incorrect. Error in applying Pythagorean theorem for orthogonal components.

questions.topic: Conservation of Momentum in 2D - Direction of Third Piece
questions.q: In boiler explosion problem, what angle does velocity vector of third piece form relative to extension of opposite direction of first two orthogonal pieces' trajectories?
questions.hint: Since two orthogonal pieces have identical mass and speed, momentum components are equal, forming $45^\circ$ angle relative to each axis.
options: $45^\circ$ (lies along angle bisector opposite first two pieces)
explanations: Correct! Since momentum components of first two fragments are identical ($p_x = p_y = m \cdot 9$), resultant vector lies along plane angle bisector (forming $45^\circ$ angle). To conserve momentum, third piece must move opposite to this bisector ($45^\circ$).
Incorrect. Angle of $30^\circ$ would occur only if one fragment had larger mass or speed than other.
Incorrect. Angle of $60^\circ$ assumes asymmetry in momentum magnitudes of perpendicular fragments.

questions.topic: Horizontal Inelastic Collision - Sled and Package
questions.q: A package of mass $m = 6\text{ kg}$ is dropped onto a sled of mass $M = 12\text{ kg}$ sliding at $9\text{ m/s}$. What will be new sled speed $v_f$?
questions.hint: Vertical fall of package adds no horizontal momentum. Initial horizontal momentum is conserved: $M v_1 = (M + m) v_f$.
explanations: Correct! By horizontal momentum conservation: $M v_1 = (M + m) v_f \implies v_f = \frac{12 \cdot 9}{12 + 6} = \frac{108}{18} = 6\text{ m/s}$.
Incorrect. $4.5\text{ m/s}$ obtained by incorrectly assuming package mass equals sled mass ($12\text{ kg}$).
Incorrect. Proportion error between total mass and initial mass.
